rationale: The book's core — that righteousness names right-living (conformity to God's ways, which for creatures under His authority is the keeping of His commandments), given and reckoned by grace but never a relabeling of wrong-living as right — explains every text printed with the entry without strain, while the strongest specific rival (forensic imputed-status righteousness as the term's primary referent) must either ignore or bifurcate away Deut 6:25, Ps 119:172, 1 John 3:7, Deut 32:4, and Ps 145:17. The book does not deny reckoning by grace; it locates the mechanism in Rom 4:7-8's own definition (iniquities forgiven, sins covered, sin not imputed) and in the exclusion of wage-claims (Rom 4:4 with Luke 17:10), a reading already accepted as premise in the frozen Works and Faith findings. The forensic counter cannot account for God's own righteousness (Deut 32:4; Ps 145:17 — righteous in ways and works, where imputation is meaningless), for Deut 6:25's explicit predication ('it shall be our righteousness, if we observe to do all these commandments'), or for 1 John 3:7's explicit anti-deception warning that doing righteousness is what constitutes being righteous. The book explains the counter's proof-texts; the counter does not explain the book's. No supplied text contradicts the book's core.
book_core_identification: Righteousness is right-living: God is Right-Living by definition (His ways and works are the measure of right), and for those under His authority righteousness is the doing of His commandments — a substance of conduct that is granted and reckoned by grace (its source is gift) but is never a bare status that renames wrong-living right.
book_secondary_elaborations: Romans 4 excludes labor presented for wages that would put God in debt, not obedience as such; even complete obedience earns no wage (Luke 17:7-10)
The reckoning of righteousness operates by forgiveness and covering of sin (Rom 4:7-8), not by transfer of a status detached from life
Righteousness is worn as the garment of righteous acts (dikaiōmata, Rev 19:8) — granted, then worn, and kept clean
Cross-referenced vocabulary system: Paul's wage/debt/law/works distinctions in The End of the Law; the four covenant-response words in ch. 6
strongest_counter_interpretation: Classic forensic imputation: 'righteousness' in its decisive soteriological use is a legal status — Christ's righteousness credited to the believer's account through faith, declared rather than lived — as evidenced by Rom 4:5-6 (God 'imputeth righteousness without works' to 'him that worketh not'), Phil 3:9 (a righteousness expressly 'not mine own, which is of the law'), and the declarative sense of dikaioō in justification contexts. Old Testament conduct-texts are then assigned to a distinct ethical sense of the word, so that Pauline righteousness and Deuteronomic righteousness are two different referents sharing one term.
counter_core_identification: Righteousness, in the sense that matters for standing before God, is a conferred forensic status — an alien righteousness credited by faith apart from any doing — not a quality or practice of right conduct in the person so counted.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that righteousness's substance is right-living: it asserts that the righteousness by which a believer stands is a declared status wholly independent of conduct, such that the term's primary referent is a legal standing rather than the doing of what is right; on this reading Deut 6:25 and 1 John 3:7 speak of a different, non-saving 'righteousness' than Rom 4 and Phil 3:9.
counter_case: Rom 4:5-6: righteousness is counted to 'him that worketh not' and imputed 'without works' — on its face a status conferred apart from doing
Phil 3:9: Paul renounces 'mine own righteousness, which is of the law' in favor of 'the righteousness which is of God by faith' — apparently setting law-conduct against received righteousness
Isa 64:6 (cited in the common interpretation): human righteousnesses are filthy rags, suggesting conduct cannot constitute righteousness before God
The dikaioō word-group in Paul is widely read as declarative/courtroom language: God declares righteous, He does not describe conduct
2 Cor 5:21 and Rom 5:17-19: righteousness as something believers 'become' or receive as 'gift', consistent with credited status
book_explanatory_advantages: Deut 6:25 explicitly predicates 'our righteousness' of observing to do all the commandments — a direct definitional statement the forensic reading must reassign to a second sense of the word

Ps 119:172 ('all thy commandments are righteousness') and Ps 145:17 / Deut 32:4 define righteousness for both the law and for God Himself as ways and works — imputation cannot be what makes God righteous, so the conduct-sense must be the term's base meaning

1 John 3:7 is framed as a warning against deception ('let no man deceive you: he that doeth righteousness is righteous'), which reads most naturally as rebutting exactly the status-without-doing inference

Rev 19:8's dikaiōmata ('the righteous acts of the saints') makes the wedding garment plural, active deeds — granted ('it was given unto her') yet performed, matching the book's 'gift in source, right-living in substance'

The book explains Rom 4 from inside the passage: vv. 7-8 define the imputation as forgiveness and covering of sin, and v. 4 identifies what is excluded — the wage/debt claim — a reading anchored by Luke 17:7-10 (printed with the entry) and by the accepted prior findings on Works and Works of the law

Heb 11:8 shows Abraham's faith as obedience enacted, cohering with the accepted Faith and Belief premises that the faith counted for righteousness (Gen 15:6) is trusting faithfulness, not conduct-free assent
One unified sense of the word across both testaments, versus the counter's forced polysemy that splits Deuteronomy from Paul
counter_explanatory_advantages: Gives the most immediate surface reading of 'imputeth righteousness without works' (Rom 4:6) and 'to him that worketh not' (Rom 4:5)
Accounts naturally for Phil 3:9's own-righteousness/God's-righteousness contrast without needing the wage-claim distinction
Aligns with the declarative force many lexicons assign to dikaioō in justification contexts
decisive_sources: Deuteronomy 6:25 — righteousness explicitly defined as observing to do all the commandments
Psalm 119:172 — all thy commandments are righteousness
Deuteronomy 32:4 and Psalm 145:17 — God's righteousness consists in His ways and works, which no imputation scheme can express, fixing the term's base sense as right-living
1 John 3:7 — an explicit anti-deception warning that doing righteousness is what makes one righteous 'even as he is righteous'
Romans 4:4-8 read whole — v. 4 identifies the excluded claim as wage/debt, vv. 7-8 define the imputation as forgiveness and covering, supporting the book's mechanism
Luke 17:7-10 — complete obedience creates no wage-claim, dissolving the inference that Rom 4 opposes obedience itself
Revelation 19:8 (dikaiōmata) — the garment of righteousness is righteous acts, given and worn
Prior accepted findings on Works, Works of the law, Faith, Belief, and Love — establishing that Paul's exclusions target purchase-power, not obedience, and that saving faith is obedient faithfulness
unresolved_objections: Phil 3:9's contrast could still be pressed as excluding law-derived conduct itself rather than only self-established, wage-claiming righteousness; the entry defers full treatment to The End of the Law rather than resolving it from Phil 3 directly

The declarative sense of dikaioō in courtroom contexts (e.g., Rom 3:26, 'justifier') is not fully engaged; the book's account of the verb 'justify' as distinct from the noun's substance is implied rather than argued

Texts prominent in the common case but not in the supplied bundle (2 Cor 5:21; Rom 5:17-19; Isa 64:6 is addressed in the Garments chapter) receive only partial treatment, leaving room for a residual imputation-of-Christ's-obedience reading of those verses
